Through the Montana Department of Health and Environmental Sciences, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), has funded a study of Hardin's sewer system, which is presently over capacity (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 f). EPA recently agreed to finance a plan for the system with the understanding that if money is available when the plan is completed, EPA will fund 75 percent of construction costs.
The other major source of funding under consideration by Hardin is the Coal Board, set up by Senate Bill 87, (also known as the Coal Severance Tax). The purpose of the bill is to tax all coal mined in Montana at 30 percent of contract sales price (net of charges attributable to tax) in order to assist coal impact areas in operation and maintenance, and to set up a permanent fund for support of the state's public schools. Of total receipts, 27.5 percent is earmarked for the Local Impact and Educational Trust Accounts. Areas which receive impacts from coal development are eligible to receive up to 7/11 of this (or 17.5 percent of the total). These funds are to be distributed by the Coal Board, and at least half of the monies must be awarded to local impact area government.
Senate Bill 87 states that the Coal Board will distribute the funds on the basis of four considerations: need, degree or severity of impact, availability of funds, and degree of local effort to meet the needs. Hardin will submit three specific grant applications to the Coal Board, possibly including an application for aid to the school districts. The items to be covered in these applications will be decided at Council meetings in January and February.
